articles.title: LLM Recap for Agent Builders: Tokens, Context Windows and Sampling
articles.description: A large language model (LLM) is a neural network, usually a transformer, trained to predict the next token in a sequence. At inference time it repeatedly turns the text so far into a probability distribution over its vocabulary, picks a token, appends it and repeats. Every agent in this course uses an LLM as its reasoning engine, so its limits (context size, cost per token, randomness and lack of memory) shape every design decision.

articles.title: What Makes a System Agentic: Autonomy, Goals and the Agency Spectrum
articles.description: An agentic system is software in which a language model decides, at run time, what to do next in order to reach a goal: which tool to call, which path to take and when the task is finished. The more of the control flow the model owns, the more agentic the system is. A workflow follows steps written by a developer; an agent chooses its own steps inside the boundaries the developer sets.

articles.title: The Agent Loop: Perceive, Reason, Act
articles.description: The agent loop is the repeating cycle at the heart of every agent: perceive the current state of the environment, reason about what to do next given the goal, act by calling a tool or producing output, then observe the result and repeat. The loop ends when the goal is met or a safety condition such as a step limit, budget or error stops it.

articles.title: ReAct: Interleaving Reasoning and Acting
articles.description: ReAct (Reason + Act) is a prompting and control pattern in which the model alternates between a short natural-language reasoning trace, called a thought, and an action such as a tool call. After each action the environment returns an observation, which becomes the next input, and the cycle repeats until the model emits a final answer. The thought helps the model plan and track state, while the action grounds the next thought in real feedback so the agent corrects course instead of hallucinating a result.

articles.title: Tool and Function Calling: Giving the Model Hands
articles.description: Tool calling, also called function calling, is a mechanism in which the model is given a list of tools described by schemas and can respond not with prose but with a structured request to invoke one of them. The application executes the tool, returns the result as a message, and the model continues. It is the bridge between reasoning and action: the model decides what to call and with which arguments, while ordinary code performs the call and enforces the rules.

articles.title: Planning and Task Decomposition
articles.description: Planning is the agent skill of breaking a goal into smaller sub-tasks and deciding the order in which to do them before or while acting. Task decomposition produces the sub-tasks; a plan records their sequence and dependencies. A good plan makes progress visible, exposes parallelism and gives the agent checkpoints, but it must stay revisable because real environments return surprises that invalidate the original plan.

articles.title: Agent Memory: Short-Term Context and Long-Term Stores
articles.description: Agent memory is the information an agent can use beyond the current model call. Short-term memory is the working context of the current task: the messages, tool results and notes inside the context window. Long-term memory is anything stored outside the model, such as a vector database, key-value store or file, and read back when relevant. Memory lets an agent act consistently across many steps and many sessions, which a stateless model cannot do on its own.

articles.description: Reflection is an agent technique in which, after an attempt, the agent critiques its own output or trajectory, records the critique as feedback, and uses it to improve the next attempt. It usually runs as an actor-evaluator-reflection loop: the actor produces an answer or action, an evaluator scores it, and a reflection step writes what went wrong and how to fix it. The feedback is stored in memory so a later attempt does not repeat the same mistake.

articles.title: What Prompt Engineering Is and How LLMs Read Prompts
articles.description: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing, testing and refining the input given to a large language model (LLM) so that it reliably produces useful, correct and well-formatted output. An LLM never sees words directly: the prompt is split into tokens, converted to numbers, and the model predicts the most suitable next token again and again, each time conditioned on the prompt and everything generated so far.

articles.title: Context Windows, Token Budgets and Conversation Memory
articles.description: A context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can consider in one request, counting the system prompt, conversation history, any documents or examples, and the tokens it generates in reply. Anything outside the window is invisible to the model, so applications must decide what to include, what to compress and what to leave out.

articles.title: Sampling Controls: Temperature, Top-k and Top-p
articles.description: Sampling controls decide how a model picks the next token from its predicted probability distribution. Temperature sharpens or flattens the distribution, top-k keeps only the k most likely tokens, and top-p (nucleus sampling) keeps the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p. Together with the prompt, these settings determine how focused or varied the output is.

Statistics uses data to estimate those probabilities and the parameters of distributions. Machine learning models are statistical models: a classifier outputs a probability distribution over classes and training chooses the parameters that make the observed data most likely.

Each step has typical failure modes, and most real-world ML failures come from data and process mistakes rather than from the choice of algorithm.

articles.title: What Vibe Coding Is: Promise, Workflow and Risks
articles.description: Vibe coding is a style of building software where you describe what you want in natural language and let an AI assistant write most of the code, judging progress mainly by whether the result runs and looks right. The term was popularised by Andrej Karpathy in early 2025. In professional settings it is a starting point: engineers still own the code, so they read, test and review what the AI produces before it ships.

articles.title: How AI Coding Assistants Work: Tokens, Context and Prediction
articles.description: An AI coding assistant is an application built on a large language model (LLM), a neural network trained on huge amounts of text and code to predict the next token given the tokens before it. The assistant collects relevant context (your prompt, open files, project rules, search results), sends it to the model, and turns the predicted tokens into suggestions, chat answers or file edits. The model has no live view of your project beyond what fits in that context.

articles.title: HTML Semantics and Document Structure
articles.description: Semantic HTML means choosing elements for what content is, not how it looks: a navigation menu goes in nav, the primary content in main, a clickable action in button, and section titles in h1–h6. Browsers, search engines and assistive technologies such as screen readers use these meanings to understand and navigate the page. Styling is applied separately with CSS.

articles.title: CSS Layout: Box Model, Flexbox and Grid
articles.description: CSS layout is how the browser sizes and positions boxes. Every element is a box made of content, padding, border and margin (the box model). Flexbox arranges items along a single axis (a row or a column) and distributes spare space between them, while CSS grid places items into rows and columns at the same time. Together they replace older float- and table-based layouts.

articles.title: Python Data Types and Core Structures for Analysts
articles.description: Python data types describe what kind of value a variable holds and which operations are allowed on it. Analysts work mostly with numbers (int, float), text (str), true/false flags (bool), the missing marker None, and four containers: list (ordered, changeable), tuple (ordered, fixed), dict (key to value lookup) and set (unique items). pandas and NumPy are built on top of these ideas, so understanding them explains much of how those libraries behave.

articles.title: Lists, Dictionaries and Comprehensions for Data Wrangling
articles.description: A comprehension is a compact Python expression that builds a new list, dict or set by looping over an iterable, optionally filtering items with a condition. Combined with dictionaries for grouping and counting, comprehensions let an analyst reshape small datasets in a few readable lines, which is exactly what pandas later does at scale.

articles.title: Functions, Lambdas and Reusable Analysis Code
articles.description: A function is a named, reusable block of code that takes inputs (parameters), performs a task and returns a result. A lambda is a small anonymous function written in one expression, typically passed to another function such as sorted or DataFrame.apply. Packaging analysis steps as functions makes notebooks reproducible and lets the same logic run on new data.

articles.title: File Handling: Reading and Writing CSV and JSON
articles.description: File handling is reading data from and writing data to files on disk. CSV (comma-separated values) stores a table as plain text, one row per line, while JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) stores nested objects and arrays. Python's built-in csv and json modules parse these formats correctly, and pandas wraps them in read_csv, read_json, to_csv and to_json for table-shaped data.

articles.title: How the Web Works: HTTP, DNS and Client-Server Architecture
articles.description: The web is a client-server system: a client such as a browser sends an HTTP request to a server, and the server returns an HTTP response. HTTP is a stateless, text-based application protocol (binary-framed in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3) that runs over TCP or QUIC, usually wrapped in TLS as HTTPS. articles.title: Modern JavaScript (ES6+): Scope, Closures and Array Methods
articles.description: ES6 (ECMAScript 2015) and later versions added block-scoped variables, arrow functions, classes, modules, destructuring, spread syntax, promises and many array and object helpers to JavaScript. A closure is a function bundled with the variables of the scope it was created in, so it can read and update those variables even after the outer function has returned.

articles.title: Asynchronous JavaScript: Event Loop, Promises and async/await
articles.description: JavaScript runs your code on a single thread, so long operations such as network requests, timers and file reads are handed to the environment (the browser or Node.js) and their results come back later as queued callbacks. The event loop runs those callbacks when the call stack is empty. A Promise represents a value that will be available in the future, and async/await is syntax that lets you write promise-based code in a readable, top-to-bottom style.

articles.title: Functions, Arguments, Scope and Closures
articles.description: A function is a named, reusable block of code defined with def that takes parameters and returns a value (None if no return runs). articles.title: Built-in Data Structures and Comprehensions
articles.description: Python's built-in data structures are list (ordered, mutable sequence), tuple (ordered, immutable sequence), dict (insertion-ordered mapping of hashable keys to values, backed by a hash table) and set (unordered collection of unique hashable items). articles.title: Numbers and Strings: Slicing, Formatting and Methods

articles.title: Operators, Expressions and Precedence

articles.title: Control Flow: Conditionals, Loops and Loop Control

articles.title: Functions: Parameters, Arguments and Return Values

articles.title: Scope, Namespaces and Closures

articles.title: Cloud Computing Concepts and the AWS Shared Responsibility Model
articles.description: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, databases, networking and other IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Instead of buying and running data-centre hardware, you rent capacity from a provider such as AWS, provision it in minutes through an API, and release it when you no longer need it. Security in the cloud is split between AWS (security OF the cloud) and the customer (security IN the cloud): this split is the shared responsibility model.

articles.title: The AWS Well-Architected Framework: Six Pillars of Good Design
articles.description: The AWS Well-Architected Framework is a set of design principles, questions and best practices for building secure, reliable, efficient, cost-effective and sustainable systems on AWS. It is organised into six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization and Sustainability. Architects use it both to design new workloads and to review existing ones for risk.

articles.title: Cloud Computing and Azure Global Infrastructure
articles.description: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of compute, storage, networking and software over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Microsoft Azure is Microsoft's public cloud: a global network of datacentres grouped into regions, on which you create resources through a single management layer instead of buying and racking your own hardware.

articles.title: Azure Resource Manager: Management Groups, Subscriptions and Resource Groups
articles.description: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the deployment and management service for Azure: every request from the portal, CLI, PowerShell, SDKs or templates is authenticated, authorised and then sent by ARM to the right resource provider. ARM organises resources in a hierarchy of management groups, subscriptions, resource groups and resources, and access control, policy and budgets applied at one level are inherited by everything beneath it.

articles.title: Tags and Resource Locks for Organising and Protecting Resources
articles.description: Tags are name-value pairs attached to Azure resources, resource groups and subscriptions to add metadata such as cost centre, environment or owner. Resource locks are management-plane safeguards that prevent accidental deletion (CanNotDelete) or any change (ReadOnly) to a scope and everything beneath it, regardless of the user's RBAC role.

articles.title: Azure Management Tools: Portal, Cloud Shell, Azure CLI and PowerShell
articles.description: Azure offers several front ends to the same Azure Resource Manager API: the web-based Azure portal, the cross-platform Azure CLI (az commands), the Azure PowerShell Az module (Verb-AzNoun cmdlets) and Azure Cloud Shell, a browser-based shell with both tools pre-installed and already signed in. Because they all call ARM, anything created with one can be managed with another.
